h1: Finding an Indian partner for a drinks brand
title: Finding an Indian Partner for a Brand | Craft Beer School
desc: How to find, check and agree terms with an Indian partner for a drinks brand: what to look for, what to verify and what an agreement should settle.
teaser: In India the partner often matters more than the product. Choose slowly.
standfirst: Most foreign drinks brands need a local partner for licences, distribution or production. This guide covers what kinds of partner exist, how to check them and what to settle in writing.
sections: What kind of partner do you need?

Start by naming the gap. A partner can fill one of four roles. A producer makes the drink in India. A distributor holds licences and moves the product to shops and bars. A licence holder carries the state registrations and legal responsibility. A joint venture partner shares ownership and risk.

Some partners do more than one. Be wary of anyone who claims to do everything in every state. Alcohol is a state subject. Licences and routes to market differ from state to state, so a partner strong in one state may have little reach in another.

Begin with the trade. Producers, distributors, licensed hotels and restaurants know who is reliable. Industry associations and trade fairs bring people together. Licensing advisers and lawyers often know both sides of a deal. Your own network, including suppliers who already sell in India, can introduce you.

A consultant can run the search for you, but treat any shortlist as a start. You still need to meet the people. We help brands define the role, build a shortlist and prepare the questions. We do not receive payment from partners and we do not guarantee that a deal will happen.

Check the facts you can verify. Ask for the company registration, the licences it holds in each state and the brands it works with. Ask whether any licence is under dispute. A licensing adviser can confirm what is current, since licences are state records and change.

Check the track record. Speak to two or three of their existing brand owners without the partner in the room. Ask how payments were handled, how quality was kept and what happened in a bad month.

Visit the plant or the warehouse if you can, or ask for a live video walk-through. Look at cleanliness, records, storage conditions and stock. A distributor who cannot show you where your product will sit is not ready for it.

Check finances sensibly. A partner who pays late can starve a young brand of cash. Ask for references from suppliers.

• The scope: which products, which states and for how long
  • Who owns the brand, the recipe and any trademarks, with registration in the right name
  • Quality standards, sampling, inspection rights and what happens to failed batches
  • Pricing: who sets ex-works and shelf prices and how changes are made
  • Minimum volumes, payment terms and stock responsibilities
  • Licences: who holds which and who answers to the state authority
  • Exclusivity, including what the partner may not sell alongside your brand
  • Exit: how either side ends the relationship and what happens to stock and the brand

Take legal advice from a lawyer who works in India and in your home country. This guide is not legal advice.

A partner who promises huge volumes in months without showing how. One who will not share licence details. One who asks for the exclusive right to all of India on day one. One who cannot explain the state rules in the states they cover.

Also watch the cultural fit. Communication habits, expectations of speed and views on quality differ between companies. A few honest conversations early save a lot of frustration later.

A first meeting that tells you something

Meet in person if you can, ideally at the partner's own site. Ask them to describe a problem they had with another brand and how they solved it. The answer shows honesty and how they work under pressure.

Ask what they would need from you in the first six months. A partner who expects support, samples and marketing material is realistic. One who needs nothing is probably not planning much.

Agree a small first step before any long contract: a trial order, a pilot in one city or a limited period. Let both sides see how the relationship works in practice.
faqs: Do I need an Indian partner at all?
Most foreign brands do, because licences and distribution are handled state by state. Some set up their own Indian company, which still needs local expertise.
Can one partner cover all of India?
Rarely. Alcohol rules are set by each state, so partners are usually strong in some states and weak in others.
Only for a defined scope, a set period and clear performance targets. Take legal advice before you agree.
